description: Your grip is only as strong as the wrist it hangs from, and a simple stick exposes the truth in a minute. Today you lever a broom handle against gravity, meet the wrist tendons that form the platform for every grip you own, and start reinforcing them.

beats.text: GRAB A BROOM BY THE END

scenes.narration: Take a broom or a mop and grip it by the very end of the handle, the way you would hold a sword by the blade end. Straighten that arm out in front of you at shoulder height, broom pointing forward like a long nose. Now, using only your wrist, raise the tip of the broom upward slowly, then lower it back down with control. That is one rep. Your forearm stays pointing forward the whole time. Count how many clean raises you manage in sixty seconds, then switch hands and count again. The smaller number is the truth, as always. Write it down. At the end of this video I will tell you what it says about the platform underneath every grip you will ever make.

scenes.label: THE LINE BETWEEN WOBBLY AND STEEL
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Ten clean lever raises in a minute is where a wobbly wrist becomes a steel platform. Under six, the tendons crossing your wrist are stabilizers in name only, and every heavy thing you grip is being held by a joint that folds under load. Over sixteen, you own the kind of wrist that climbers, gymnasts and arm wrestlers build their whole game on. Notice the genius of this test. The broom weighs almost nothing. The lever makes it honest. A meter of handle multiplies a tiny weight into a serious tendon exam, and there is no way to cheat a lever.
scenes.sub: under 6: platform folds - over 16: steel platform

beats.label: OF GRIP FORCE IS WRIST POSITION

scenes.narration: Look at your wrist and count what crosses it. Every tendon that closes your fingers passes through this one narrow joint on its way to the forearm. But there is a second crew, less famous and just as important: the wrist tendons themselves, whose job is not to move the hand but to hold the wrist in position while the fingers work. Grip researchers have shown for decades that your fingers are strongest when the wrist is held slightly extended, locked in its powerful position, and dramatically weaker when the wrist flops forward or bends back. In other words, your grip strength is not really in your fingers. It is rented from your wrist position. If the platform holds, the fingers can pull with everything they have. If the platform folds a few degrees, the finger tendons lose their angle and a third of your grip quietly evaporates. Your lever test grades the platform crew directly, with no fingers involved at all. That is why it predicts your real-world grip better than a squeeze test does. Think of the last heavy bag you carried by its handles. Your fingers did not open first. Your wrist started to bend, the angle leaked, and only then did the fingers give up. The platform always fails before the grip does. It just fails quietly, a few degrees at a time, so nobody ever blames it.

Let us appreciate the physics of the stick for a moment, because it is the cheapest laboratory in this entire series. Torque is force multiplied by distance. A broom weighs perhaps half a kilo, which sounds like nothing. But grip it at the very end and that half kilo hangs a meter from your wrist, and the tendons experience it like a serious weight. Slide your hand just twenty centimeters up the handle and the exam gets dramatically easier, which is why choking up on the grip is the oldest cheat in this test. This is also why the lever test scales forever. As your number climbs, you do not need heavier equipment. You need a longer stick, or a slower tempo, and the same half kilo becomes a new exam. Gyms sell machines to do this. You own a broom. The physics does not care which one you use, and neither do your tendons.

beats.title: UP IS ONLY HALF THE TEST

beats.label: OF WRIST STRENGTH IS CONTROL DOWN

scenes.narration: One detail separates a good wrist from a complete one. Raising the tip trains the tendons on the back of the forearm, the extensors. Lowering it slowly is where the front crew, the flexors, earns its keep, braking the lever against gravity. Most people only ever train the raising half, in every exercise they do, and then wonder why their wrist feels strong in one direction and treacherous in the other. Real-world grips do not ask permission about direction. A heavy bag twists down. A bar pulls down. A climbing hold drags the wrist wherever it wants. The platform has to hold in every direction at once, which is why this test counts only reps that are controlled on the way down. Own the whole arc, up and down, and the joint stops having a weak side for the world to find.

lines: how big the arm above it is.
beats.title: YOUR BUILD IS NO EXCUSE

scenes.narration: Here is the skinny advantage at the wrist, and it might be the purest one in this series. The wrist tendons do not know how big the arm above them is. They know torque, angle and time, and all three are identical for you and for a man twice your size holding the same broom. Big forearms look like grip strength, but the platform underneath them is built from the same small tendons you have, trained or untrained. Plenty of huge men fold at rep five of this test because nobody ever examined their platform. You can own a top-percentile wrist with a broom, a minute, and a month of attendance, while the big guys keep squeezing harder on a folding foundation.

Now we build the platform together. Broom at the end grip, arm straight, raise and lower with control. Thirty seconds, rest, switch hands. Four rounds, two per side. The forearm never twists. If the tip starts swinging, slow down. Go.

Here is your week. The four rounds you just did, every other day, weak hand first, matching reps on the strong hand. Now the mistakes. Mistake one: choking up the handle when it gets hard. That is not a modification, it is a different, easier test. If you cannot finish at the end grip, rest longer. Mistake two: twisting the forearm to help the tip rise. The moment the forearm rotates, the big rotation muscles steal the job from the wrist crew. Mistake three: rushing the lowering. The way down is half the training, and dropping it is like doing half a push-up forever. One extra clean rep a week is the pace. The platform is small, it adapts fast, and it will change every grip you own when it does.

scenes.label: RETEST - SAME BROOM, END GRIP
scenes.narration: So, your number, grading the weaker hand as always. Under six: the platform folds, and your grip has been leaking force at the wrist your whole life without telling you. Six to ten: the crew is waking up, and everyday grips already feel different. Over ten: a trained platform that holds its angle under load. Over sixteen: steel, the kind of wrist that makes every other grip test easier. Put the smaller number in the comments. Just the reps. In thirty days we take the broom down again and re-grade the platform.
scenes.sub: comment your smaller number - then beat it

scenes.narration: Thirty days from now the broom comes off the wall again, and a meter of wood will report what your wrists became. Subscribe so the retest finds you, and leave the smaller number in the comments where you cannot hide from it. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Why Your wrist tendons Matter More Than Muscle (The wrist tendon training Episode)
